Can You Have Dental Implants While Undergoing Fertility Treatment or IVF?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Many people who are planning or actively undergoing fertility treatment, including IVF, find themselves wondering whether it is safe to proceed with dental implant treatment at the same time. It is a genuinely thoughtful question, and one that arises more frequently than you might expect, particularly as more adults seek restorative dental care alongside other medical procedures.

Dental implants during IVF and fertility treatment is a topic that sits at the intersection of oral health and reproductive medicine, and it deserves a careful, balanced discussion. The motivations behind the question are entirely understandable — many patients do not want to delay dental treatment unnecessarily, whilst others are rightly cautious about combining invasive procedures during a physically and emotionally demanding time.

This article aims to provide clear, educational guidance on what is currently understood about dental implants in the context of fertility treatment and IVF, what factors clinicians typically consider, and why individual clinical assessment is always essential before making any decisions. Whether you are at the early stages of fertility planning or actively mid-cycle, understanding the relevant oral health considerations can help you have a more informed conversation with your dental and medical teams.

Dental implants during IVF or fertility treatment are generally not recommended without careful coordination between your dental and medical teams. Implant surgery involves anaesthesia, antibiotics, and a healing period that may interact with fertility medications or hormonal changes. Timing and individual health status should always be assessed clinically before proceeding.

Understanding Dental Implants: A Brief Overview

Before exploring the relationship between dental implants and fertility treatment, it is helpful to understand what dental implant treatment involves clinically.

A dental implant is a small titanium post that is surgically placed into the jawbone to replace the root of a missing tooth. Over a period of weeks to months, the implant integrates with the surrounding bone through a process called osseointegration. Once this integration is complete, a dental crown or prosthetic tooth is attached to the implant, restoring both the appearance and function of the missing tooth.

The treatment process typically involves several stages: an initial consultation and assessment (including imaging such as a CBCT scan), the surgical placement procedure itself, a healing period, and the final restoration phase. Depending on the patient's clinical situation, the overall timeline can range from a few months to over a year.

Implant surgery is generally performed under local anaesthesia. Post-operative care frequently involves a short course of antibiotics to reduce infection risk and analgesics for pain management. These factors — the surgical nature of the procedure, the medications involved, and the need for a settled healing environment — are directly relevant when considering timing alongside fertility treatment.

If you would like to learn more about what the treatment involves, our single tooth implant treatment guide provides a detailed overview of the stages involved.

Why Timing Matters: Fertility Treatment and the Body's Response

Fertility treatment, particularly IVF (in vitro fertilisation), places significant physical and hormonal demands on the body. The protocols typically involve carefully controlled cycles of hormonal stimulation, egg retrieval, embryo transfer, and — in many cases — additional hormonal support during the luteal phase or early pregnancy.

These hormonal fluctuations are not merely a background consideration. Elevated levels of oestrogen and progesterone during fertility treatment are known to affect oral tissues. Research has indicated that hormonal changes can increase the inflammatory response of gum tissue, making the gums more susceptible to irritation, bleeding, and sensitivity. This is a similar phenomenon to the oral changes sometimes observed during natural pregnancy.

From a dental implant perspective, the ideal conditions for successful osseointegration include a stable immune environment, good bone health, and controlled systemic health. Hormonal variation during IVF cycles can theoretically influence the body's healing response, though robust clinical evidence specifically examining dental implant outcomes during IVF is limited at present.

Additionally, the psychological and emotional demands of fertility treatment are significant. Many patients and clinicians agree that reducing additional physical stressors during an IVF cycle is prudent where possible, not from a position of alarm, but from a sensible commitment to patient-centred care.

Medications Used in Fertility Treatment: Considerations for Dental Care

One of the more clinically specific areas of concern relates to the medications used during IVF and fertility treatment protocols. These may include:

  • Gonadotrophin injections (used to stimulate egg production)
  • GnRH agonists or antagonists (to control ovulation timing)
  • Progesterone supplements (to support implantation)
  • Anticoagulants (sometimes prescribed alongside fertility protocols in specific cases)
  • Steroids (used in certain IVF protocols to modulate immune response)

Several of these medications carry considerations relevant to dental implant surgery. Anticoagulants can affect bleeding time during and after surgery. Corticosteroids can influence healing and immune response. Some hormonal medications may affect bone metabolism, which is directly relevant to the osseointegration process.

It is also worth noting that antibiotics are commonly prescribed after dental implant surgery to minimise infection risk. The interaction between such antibiotics and fertility medications is something that should be reviewed by both your dental clinician and your reproductive medicine specialist before any treatment commences.

This does not mean that dental implant treatment is categorically incompatible with fertility medications — rather, it means that both clinical teams need to communicate and that individual circumstances must be carefully evaluated.

Clinical Guidance: What Most Dental Clinicians Would Advise

In the absence of a specific medical emergency, most experienced implant dentists in the UK would advise against scheduling elective dental implant surgery during an active IVF cycle. This recommendation is rooted in a precautionary, patient-centred approach rather than any absolute contraindication.

The key periods of concern are typically:

  • During hormonal stimulation phase — the body is under significant hormonal stress, and any additional surgical recovery may be burdensome.
  • Around egg retrieval — this is itself a minor surgical procedure, and combining recoveries is generally inadvisable.
  • During embryo transfer and the two-week wait — this is a physically and emotionally sensitive period where minimising additional procedures is considered best practice.
  • During confirmed early pregnancy — if IVF results in a confirmed pregnancy, elective dental surgery is typically deferred, particularly during the first trimester.

Between IVF cycles, or prior to commencing a fertility protocol, dental implant consultations and even implant placement may be feasible — provided that the patient's overall health, healing capacity, and medication status are suitable. However, this should always be confirmed through proper clinical dialogue between your dental team and your fertility specialist.

The Science Behind Osseointegration and Hormonal Health

To understand why hormonal health is relevant to dental implants, it is useful to appreciate the biological process of osseointegration in a little more detail.

When a titanium implant post is placed into the jawbone, the surrounding bone tissue begins to respond. Specialised bone cells — osteoblasts — start to lay down new bone matrix around the implant surface, gradually anchoring it securely. This process is sensitive to a range of systemic factors, including blood supply to the area, immune function, the presence of infection, nutritional status, and hormonal balance.

Oestrogen, in particular, has a known influence on bone metabolism. Oestrogen helps regulate bone turnover, and during fertility treatment where oestrogen levels are artificially elevated, there may be subtle effects on the bone remodelling process. Similarly, conditions that affect bone density — such as those sometimes associated with fertility challenges — may influence implant success rates.

It is important to emphasise that many patients successfully receive dental implants during various stages of hormonal health changes, including the natural hormonal fluctuations associated with the menstrual cycle. The concern with IVF is more about the intensity and rapidity of hormonal change, combined with the medications involved, rather than any inherent incompatibility between the two treatments.

Your implant dentist will typically assess bone density and quality through imaging before proceeding, and any systemic health factors — including reproductive health history — would form part of a thorough clinical assessment.

Oral Health Changes During Fertility Treatment

Many patients undergoing fertility treatment notice changes to their oral health that they may not initially associate with their medications or hormonal changes. These can include:

  • Increased gum sensitivity or bleeding when brushing and flossing
  • Mild gum swelling or puffiness
  • Heightened tooth sensitivity
  • Changes in saliva consistency
  • Occasional mouth ulcers

These changes are generally not cause for alarm, but they are worth discussing with your dental team. They reflect the impact of hormonal fluctuation on the soft tissues of the mouth, and they highlight the importance of maintaining excellent oral hygiene throughout any fertility treatment journey.

Good periodontal (gum) health is also considered an important factor in dental implant success. Unhealthy gums or active gum disease would typically need to be treated before implant placement could be considered. If fertility treatment has temporarily affected gum health, your dentist may recommend that these issues are resolved before proceeding with any implant planning.

If post-surgical recovery symptoms are part of your concern, this explainer on why an implant site can feel warm or throb after surgery may help with expectations.

When to Seek Professional Dental Assessment

There are certain situations where seeking dental advice promptly during fertility treatment is important, regardless of implant planning:

  • Dental pain or toothache that does not resolve within a day or two
  • Swelling of the face, jaw, or gums
  • Signs of dental infection, such as a bad taste, pus, or fever
  • Trauma to a tooth following an accident or fall
  • A broken or loose existing dental restoration

If you experience any of these issues, you should contact your dental team promptly. Untreated dental infections carry their own risks to general health, and in the context of fertility treatment, addressing oral health issues is important. Emergency dental care can usually be adapted to minimise risk even during a fertility cycle, but your dentist will need to be fully informed about your current medications and treatment stage.

It is worth noting that dental X-rays, when clinically necessary, use very low doses of radiation and are not considered to pose a meaningful risk. However, as a general precaution, non-emergency dental imaging may be deferred if you are in the two-week wait following embryo transfer until a pregnancy result is confirmed.

Prevention and Oral Health Advice During Fertility Treatment

Maintaining excellent oral health during fertility treatment is entirely achievable with some thoughtful daily habits. The following practical steps can help support both gum health and overall oral hygiene during this time:

Maintain a consistent oral hygiene routine. Brush twice daily with a fluoride toothpaste and clean between your teeth with floss or interdental brushes. This becomes even more important if you notice increased gum sensitivity.

Stay well hydrated. Fertility medications can sometimes affect saliva production. Adequate water intake helps maintain a healthy oral environment.

Attend routine dental check-ups before commencing a fertility cycle if possible. Addressing any outstanding dental treatment before your IVF cycle begins means you are less likely to encounter dental emergencies during the most sensitive phases.

Inform both your dental team and fertility specialist of all medications. A complete and up-to-date medication list ensures that both teams can make appropriate clinical decisions on your behalf.

Avoid unnecessary elective dental procedures during active IVF cycles. Routine check-ups and hygiene appointments are generally acceptable, but major restorative or surgical work is best planned around your cycle.

For those already planning implant treatment, exploring dental implant planning and consultation options with your dentist well in advance of commencing a fertility cycle is a sensible step.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants during IVF or fertility treatment are generally not recommended during active treatment cycles without careful coordination between your dental and medical teams.
  • Hormonal changes during fertility treatment can temporarily affect gum health and may influence healing responses.
  • Medications used in IVF protocols — including anticoagulants, steroids, and hormonal agents — may have implications for surgical dental procedures.
  • Urgent dental care (such as infection treatment) should not be delayed regardless of fertility treatment stage; always inform both your dentist and fertility specialist.
  • Thorough planning — ideally before commencing an IVF cycle — gives patients the best opportunity to address dental needs safely.
  • Individual clinical assessment by a qualified dental professional is essential before any treatment decision is made.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it safe to have dental X-rays during IVF treatment?

Dental X-rays involve very low doses of radiation and are generally considered safe. However, as a precautionary measure, non-urgent X-rays are often deferred during the two-week wait following embryo transfer until a pregnancy result is known. If an X-ray is clinically necessary — for example, to assess a dental infection — your dentist will use appropriate protective measures and will take into account your current treatment stage. Always inform your dental team that you are undergoing fertility treatment so that informed decisions can be made together.

Can I have a dental implant consultation during IVF?

Yes. A consultation, which typically involves a clinical examination and potentially diagnostic imaging, is very different from the surgical placement procedure itself. Attending a consultation during a fertility treatment cycle is entirely reasonable and can be valuable for planning purposes. It allows your dental team to assess your suitability for implants, discuss timing, and prepare a treatment plan that can be executed at the most appropriate point in your reproductive health journey. No surgical commitment is required at a consultation stage.

What happens if I need a dental extraction during IVF?

If you need an emergency dental extraction during an IVF cycle, your dentist will assess whether it can be safely performed given your current medications and health status. Urgent dental extractions are generally carried out even during fertility treatment when necessary, as untreated dental infections pose their own risks. Your dentist and fertility specialist should communicate to ensure that the anaesthetic used and any prescribed antibiotics are appropriate alongside your fertility medications. Non-urgent extractions are usually best deferred to between cycles where possible.

How long should I wait after IVF before having dental implants?

There is no universal waiting period, as this depends entirely on individual circumstances. If an IVF cycle does not result in pregnancy, patients typically wait until they have recovered physically and emotionally before planning elective procedures. If a pregnancy is confirmed, most clinicians would advise deferring elective implant surgery until after the birth and postnatal recovery. Between cycles, implant treatment may be feasible depending on overall health and the timing of the next planned cycle. Your dental and medical teams can advise on the most appropriate timeline for your specific situation.

Does fertility treatment affect gum health?

Yes, hormonal changes associated with fertility treatment — particularly elevated oestrogen and progesterone levels — can temporarily affect gum tissue. Gums may become more sensitive, prone to bleeding, or slightly swollen during periods of hormonal fluctuation. This is similar to the gum changes sometimes seen during pregnancy. These effects are generally temporary and manageable with good oral hygiene. Informing your dentist that you are undergoing fertility treatment allows them to provide tailored advice and monitor your gum health appropriately throughout the process.

Can antibiotics prescribed after dental implant surgery affect IVF success?

This is a question that should be discussed directly with both your dental clinician and your fertility specialist. Certain antibiotics are commonly prescribed after implant surgery to reduce the risk of infection. Some antibiotics may interact with fertility medications or, in theory, affect the hormonal environment in ways that could be relevant during an active IVF cycle. This does not mean that antibiotics are categorically harmful to IVF outcomes, but it underscores the importance of both clinical teams being fully informed and coordinating care appropriately before any treatment proceeds.

Conclusion

The question of whether dental implants and fertility treatment or IVF can safely coexist is one that warrants thoughtful, individualised consideration. Whilst dental implants are a well-established and effective long-term solution for missing teeth, the timing of the procedure matters greatly, particularly when the body is simultaneously navigating the physical and hormonal demands of assisted reproduction.

The general clinical consensus is that elective implant surgery is best planned outside of active IVF cycles, ideally before a fertility cycle begins or between cycles, in order to support the best possible conditions for both osseointegration and reproductive health. However, urgent dental care should never be delayed regardless of fertility treatment stage, and maintaining excellent oral hygiene throughout is always beneficial.

Open communication between your dental team and fertility specialist is essential. Both teams need to be aware of the medications you are taking, the stage of your treatment, and any symptoms you are experiencing to make safe, appropriate clinical decisions.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

In the UK, patients may wish to confirm that their treating clinician is listed on the General Dental Council (GDC) register and that the provider is regulated by the Care Quality Commission (CQC), where applicable. No treatment outcome can be guaranteed, and suitability and expected results vary by individual clinical assessment.

If you have concerns about your oral health or are considering dental implant treatment alongside fertility planning, we encourage you to speak with a qualified dental professional who can assess your specific circumstances and guide you accordingly. For preparation discussions with your GP and dentist, this guide on what blood test results matter before dental implant surgery is also useful.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.
